stories.title: Iran protest victim: 'They were shooting to kill'
stories.summary: In January 2026, weeks before the US and Israel launched attacks on Iran, thousands of Iranians risked their lives in the largest and most widespread public uprising the regime in Tehran had ever faced. The protests began in December 2025 amid grievances over economic hardship, but soon grew in scope and scale. The regime's security forces, made up of elements from the Ministry of Intelligence, the Basij militia, and the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), confronted the protesters on the streets with gunfire and beatings. The scale of the crackdown drew international condemnation. At one point, US President Donald Trump threatened military strikes against the regime in response, telling protesters "help is on its way." But help never came. As the ensuing war overshadowed the aftermath of the bloody crackdown, support for the Iranian public in standing up against the regime fell off of the agenda. There are no precise figures for the number of people killed or injured in the January 2026 protests. Iranian authorities have put the death toll at over 3,100. However, Amnesty International stresses that because of the internet shutdown during the protests, the scale of the crackdown, and pressure on victims' families, the actual number of deaths is likely to be much higher. The US-based Human Rights Activists in Iran (HRANA) confirmed over 7,000 deaths and investigated thousands more. Seven months after the bloody crackdown, victims are dealing with permanent physical disability along with losing the opportunity to work or get an education.

stories.title: Algeria’s schools put Shakespeare before Molière in break from France
stories.summary: Algerian primary schools will begin teaching English before French for the first time, signalling the country’s break from France. Ahmed Krim spent 30 years teaching English in Algeria’s middle schools. Now retired, the 60-year-old watched the language he loved remain firmly behind French as the country’s second language. English was less valued than French, which might have been the language of Algeria’s coloniser, but continues to be present in every dialogue, six decades after independence. On July 25, Algeria’s Education Minister, Mohamed Seghir Saadaoui, announced that English will become the sole foreign language taught in the third year of primary school in the new academic year for 2026-2027. French would be pushed back to the fourth year, ending its domination of foreign language classes in Algerian schools. From next month, eight-year-olds across Algeria will become the first to learn English before French. “It is a very good decision. But it requires thinking, planning and resources,” Krim told Al Jazeera. It is among the first steps in President Abdelmadjid Tebboune’s linguistic overhaul for Algeria, which he first outlined in 2022 with English being introduced to primary schools. Since then, medicine and science faculties have begun switching from French to English. The French language has been erased from some utility bills and Air Algerie tickets.
